title: Foundations of Scientific Writing

body.text: What scientific writing is for, and how a paper is built
Scientific Writing: Principles and Practice · Honours Student Program

title: By the End of Today, You Can:

items: Explain why scientific writing has its own rules — and why those rules exist
Name the major types of scientific documents and what each is for
Describe the IMRAD structure and what belongs in each section
Recognize the parts and purpose of a title and an abstract
A way of reporting research so that other people can understand it, judge it, and build on it
It is not just 'formal English' — it follows a logic that mirrors the scientific method itself
Every choice — structure, tense, word order — exists to help a reader evaluate your evidence quickly and fairly
As an Honours student, this is the skill that turns your research into something the field can actually use

body.text: Peer Researchers
Need enough detail to replicate your method and trust your results
Reviewers & Editors
Judge rigor, novelty, and whether the claims match the evidence
Clinicians
Want to know: does this change what I do for my patients?
The Public & Policy Makers
Rely on plain-language summaries to make real-world decisions

title: Think of a paper or report you found hard to read. What exactly made it difficult?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor — 90 seconds, then we'll share

items: Unnecessary jargon or undefined abbreviations
Sentences carrying two or three ideas at once
Results and interpretation mixed together
No clear thread from the question to the conclusion
The structure doesn't match what the reader expects

body.text: Everyday / Creative Writing

items: Can build suspense — save the punchline
Voice and style are personal and varied
Structure is flexible, even surprising
Ambiguity can be a feature

body.text: Scientific Writing

items: States the main finding early and directly
Voice is precise, consistent, and impersonal
Structure is conventional and predictable (IMRAD)
Ambiguity is a defect to be removed

title: Which of these is NOT a core value of scientific writing?

body.text: Clarity — one idea communicated without confusion
Reproducibility — enough detail for others to repeat the work
Suspense — withholding the main finding until the end
Objectivity — separating observation from interpretation
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

title: Authorship Is a Responsibility, Not a Reward

items: Being listed as an author means you take public responsibility for the work's accuracy
Common international criteria (ICMJE) require: substantial contribution, drafting or revising the manuscript, final approval, and accountability
Contributing data collection alone, without intellectual input, is usually acknowledged — not authored
Discuss authorship early with your supervisor, not after the paper is drafted

title: Why might it matter — ethically and practically — that authorship carries real accountability?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor — 90 seconds

items: If an error or misconduct is later found, authors are the ones held responsible
This discourages 'gift authorship' — adding someone who didn't meaningfully contribute
It also protects genuine contributors: their name is tied to work they can vouch for

body.text: Original Article
Full report of a new study — the core format this course builds toward
Conference Abstract
Short summary submitted for presentation at a meeting
Review Article
Synthesizes existing literature on a defined question
Thesis / Dissertation
Extended, structured account of a full research project
Case Report
Detailed account of a single, instructive clinical case
Grant Proposal
Persuasive plan for research not yet conducted

rows: Report new data and its interpretation
Synthesize and critically evaluate prior work
Document an instructive or novel clinical case

title: Which of these have you already written — even in a rough or informal form?

body.text: Raise your hand for each one as it's named

items: Every format in the last table is a variation on the same underlying logic
The original research article is the strictest, most complete expression of that logic — so it's the best format to learn the skill from
Master IMRAD, and reviews, case reports, and theses become much easier to structure
From here on, we'll build your understanding of IMRAD section by section

title: A student wants to present preliminary pilot data at a 10-minute conference slot. Which format fits best?

body.text: A full original article
A conference abstract
A thesis chapter
A grant proposal
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

title: Other Parts of a Complete Manuscript

body.text: Title Page
Title, author list, affiliations, and corresponding author contact
References
Full citation list, formatted to the journal's required style
Acknowledgments
Credits contributors who don't meet full authorship criteria
Supplementary Material
Extra data, methods detail, or figures that support the main text
Funding Statement
Discloses who paid for the research and their role, if any
Conflict of Interest
Discloses any financial or personal interests that could bias the work

title: Why do you think journals require authors to disclose conflicts of interest and funding sources?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor — 90 seconds

items: Readers can judge whether a funding source might have shaped the study design or interpretation
It doesn't mean funded research is untrustworthy — it means readers get to decide for themselves
Undisclosed conflicts, if discovered later, can seriously damage a researcher's credibility
I — Introduction
Why did you do this study?
M — Methods
What did you do, exactly?
R — Results
What did you find?
D — Discussion
What does it mean?

body.text: IMRAD mirrors the scientific method itself: question → procedure → observation → interpretation.
Title
One sentence, the whole paper's identity
Abstract
The paper in miniature — 200–300 words
Introduction
Funnels from broad topic to your specific question
Methods
Recipe detailed enough to repeat
Results
What was observed — no interpretation
Discussion
Meaning, limits, and implications

title: What Each Section Is Responsible For

body.text: Introduction
Establishes the gap in knowledge and states your specific aim or hypothesis
Results
Reports findings objectively, ordered logically, supported by figures/tables
Methods
Describes participants, materials, and procedures in past tense, step by step
Discussion
Interprets findings, compares to prior work, states limits and significance

items: Opens with the broad clinical or scientific context — why should anyone care?
Narrows to what is already known, citing key prior work
Identifies the specific gap: what remains unknown or unresolved
Ends with your precise aim, question, or hypothesis — the narrowest point of the funnel

body.text: We'll build a full introduction, step by step, in Class 3.

items: Written so a competent researcher elsewhere could repeat your study exactly
Always past tense — you are reporting what you did, not instructing the reader
Includes participants/materials, procedures, measurements, and statistical analysis
No results and no interpretation belong here — only what was done
Reports what was observed — described in words, supported by figures and tables
Follows a logical order, usually matching the order methods were introduced
States numbers precisely: exact values, units, and appropriate statistics
The single most common student error: sneaking interpretation in here — save it for the Discussion
Opens by restating the main finding in plain terms
Compares your results to previous studies — do they agree, or not, and why?
States limitations honestly — every study has them
Closes with the real-world or scientific significance of the work

title: “Blood pressure was significantly lower in the treatment group (p<0.01).” Which IMRAD section does this sentence belong in?

body.text: Decide individually, then compare with a neighbor

items: It reports an observed finding with a statistic — no interpretation, no comparison to other studies
A Discussion version might read: “This reduction suggests the treatment improves cardiovascular risk, consistent with prior trials”
Notice the shift: Results = what happened. Discussion = what it means

body.text: MIXES IN INTERPRETATION
“The treatment group showed lower blood pressure, which proves the drug is effective and should be adopted as first-line therapy.”
“Proves” and “should be adopted” are interpretive claims — they belong in the Discussion, supported by comparison to other evidence.
STAYS OBJECTIVE
“Mean systolic blood pressure was 8 mmHg lower in the treatment group than the control group (p<0.01).”

title: Where should a study's limitations be discussed?

body.text: In the Methods, as a disclaimer
In the Results, after the main findings
In the Discussion, before the conclusion
In the Abstract only
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

rows: Why did you do this study?

title: From Draft to Publication — A Preview

body.text: Draft
Write a complete first version of the manuscript
Internal Review
Co-authors and mentors give feedback
Submit
Sent to a target journal for consideration
Peer Review
Independent experts evaluate the work
Publish
Revised and accepted version becomes public

title: The Title: Your Paper's Only Guaranteed Reader

items: Most people who encounter your paper will only ever read the title
It must be informative enough to stand alone — no vague or clever titles
Should describe the population, intervention/exposure, and key outcome where possible
Every important search term a colleague might use should appear somewhere in it

body.text: TOO VAGUE
“A Study of Blood Pressure in Patients”
The strong version names the intervention, duration, population, and outcome — a reader (or search engine) knows exactly what's inside.
SPECIFIC & SEARCHABLE
“Effect of an 8-Week Walking Program on Systolic Blood Pressure in Adults with Stage 1 Hypertension”

items: A self-contained summary — usually 200–300 words, with a strict journal word limit
Mirrors IMRAD in miniature: background, aim, methods, key results, conclusion
Must be understandable without reading the rest of the paper
Often written last, even though it appears first

body.text: Structured

items: Labeled subheadings: Background, Methods, Results, Conclusion
Common in clinical and biomedical journals
Easier to scan quickly for key facts

body.text: Unstructured

items: One continuous paragraph, no subheadings
Common in basic science and some humanities-adjacent journals
Requires stronger internal logic to guide the reader

title: If you searched a database for your own future study, what words would you type?

body.text: Jot down 3 keywords — we'll compare a few out loud

items: Include your key terms in the title, abstract, and keyword list — not just once, but naturally repeated
Avoid abbreviations or lab-specific jargon in place of standard terms
Think like your future reader, not like the person who already knows the project

title: An abstract should generally be understandable:

body.text: Only by co-authors who know the project
Only after reading the full paper
On its own, without reading the rest of the paper
Only by statisticians
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

title: Weak Abstract Opening vs. Strong Abstract Opening

body.text: GENERIC
“This study looks at an important health topic and presents some interesting findings.”
A strong abstract opening states the specific topic and why it matters — never a vague preview of “something interesting.”
SPECIFIC AND INFORMATIVE
“Background: Adherence to hypertension medication remains low among young adults, though the reasons are poorly understood.”

items: Draft it last, but budget real time for it — it's often the most-read part of your paper
Try writing one sentence per IMRAD section first, then expand within the word limit
Check your target journal's exact word limit and structure requirements before finalizing
Read it aloud once, completely alone from the rest of the paper — does it still make sense?

body.text: Scientific writing exists to help readers evaluate evidence quickly and fairly
Different documents (article, review, case report, thesis) serve different purposes
IMRAD is the shared logic behind almost all of them: question → method → finding → meaning
The title and abstract carry outsized weight — most readers never go further

title: Good scientific writing doesn't decorate an idea — it gets out of its way.

body.text: — A guiding principle for this course
Bring these to our next session

items: Find one published original article in your field of interest
Label its Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion sections
Bring one sentence from that paper's Results that you think is written clearly

eyebrow: Branko Aleksic · Dept. of International Medical Education
title: Writing Clear and Accurate Sentences

body.text: Sentence structure, voice, and cutting the words that don't earn their place
Scientific Writing: Principles and Practice · Honours Student Program

title: By the End of Today, You Can:

items: Build sentences and paragraphs that carry exactly one idea at a time
Choose actively between active and passive voice, not by habit
Recognize and remove the redundancy that clogs scientific prose
Revise a rough sentence into a clear, precise one

title: “It was found that the levels of the biomarker, which had been previously reported in several other studies conducted in different populations, were significantly elevated.” What's wrong with this sentence?

body.text: Talk with a neighbor — what would you cut first?

items: It buries the finding (“levels were elevated”) under a long qualifying clause
Passive voice (“it was found”) adds words without adding meaning
A reader has to hold three ideas in memory before reaching the point
Fix: split it. State the finding first, then add context in a second sentence

title: Four Habits of Clear Scientific Writers

body.text: One Idea, One Sentence
Never let a sentence carry more than one claim
Cut Redundancy
Every surviving word should earn its place
Deliberate Voice
Choose active or passive based on what matters
One Purpose, One Paragraph
Build paragraphs around a single topic sentence

items: Every sentence should make exactly one claim the reader can check off before moving on
If a sentence needs 'and', 'which', or 'while' to hold two unrelated facts together, consider splitting it
Short does not mean simplistic — precision is the goal, not brevity for its own sake
Long sentences are appropriate only when the ideas are genuinely, logically connected

body.text: TWO IDEAS COLLIDING
“The intervention reduced HbA1c by 0.8%, and adherence was measured using a validated questionnaire administered at baseline and follow-up.”
The result and the measurement method are two separate claims — each deserves its own sentence.
SPLIT INTO TWO CLAIMS
“The intervention reduced HbA1c by 0.8%. Adherence was measured using a validated questionnaire at baseline and follow-up.”

title: “Participants were randomized to treatment or control and the primary outcome, defined as change in systolic blood pressure at 12 weeks, was analyzed using a mixed-effects model.” How would you split this into two sentences?

body.text: Draft a two-sentence version on paper — 2 minutes

items: “Participants were randomized to treatment or control.”
“The primary outcome — change in systolic blood pressure at 12 weeks — was analyzed using a mixed-effects model.”
Notice: each sentence now answers one question a reader might ask

title: A sentence containing three linked clauses joined by 'and' is usually a sign that you should:

body.text: Add more clauses for completeness
Consider splitting it into separate sentences
Convert it to passive voice
Move it to the abstract
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

items: A nominalization turns a strong verb into an abstract noun — 'investigate' becomes 'conduct an investigation of'
This adds words and distances the sentence from a clear actor and action
Scan your drafts for endings like '-tion', '-ment', '-ance' — each is a candidate for a stronger verb
Not every nominalization is wrong — but most sentences read better with the verb restored

body.text: BURIED VERB
“The research team conducted an investigation of the relationship between diet and inflammation.”
“Conducted an investigation of” and “investigated” mean exactly the same thing — the second version says it in three fewer words.
VERB RESTORED
“The research team investigated the relationship between diet and inflammation.”
Active Voice

items: “We measured blood pressure every 4 weeks.”
Shorter, more direct, easier to follow
Best when the actor (who did it) matters

body.text: Passive Voice

items: “Blood pressure was measured every 4 weeks.”
Shifts focus onto the action or object, not the actor
Best when the actor is obvious, irrelevant, or unknown
Use active voice by default
It's shorter and puts the responsible agent front and center
Use passive voice deliberately in Methods
“Samples were centrifuged” — the reader doesn't need to know who operated the centrifuge
Avoid passive voice when it hides who is responsible for a judgment
“It is believed that...” hides whether this is your claim or someone else's
Many journals now prefer active voice throughout — check journal-specific author guidelines

title: Passive Voice That Hides the Actor

body.text: WHO DECIDED THIS?
“It was decided that the control group would not receive follow-up assessment.”
The revised version restores the actor and adds the missing reason — both are information the reader needs.
CLEAR RESPONSIBILITY
“The research team excluded the control group from follow-up assessment to reduce participant burden.”

rows: You are making claims and setting up an argument
The actor (you) is often assumed; the procedure matters more
Direct statement of what was found reads more clearly
You are the one interpreting — own that role

title: “The questionnaire was completed by participants after each session.” Rewrite this in active voice. Does it read better, or was passive the right choice?

body.text: Try both versions on paper — 90 seconds

items: Active: “Participants completed the questionnaire after each session.” — slightly shorter, equally clear
Here, either voice works well because the actor (participants) is not in question
The real test: does the voice you chose make the sentence easier or harder to follow?

title: In a Methods section, passive voice is most defensible when:

body.text: You want to sound more formal
The actor performing the action is obvious or unimportant
You are unsure who did the work
You need to lengthen the section
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

title: Hedging: Saying How Sure You Are

items: Hedges ('may', 'could', 'suggests', 'appears to') calibrate how confident a claim is
Under-hedging overstates certainty; over-hedging makes every sentence sound tentative and weak
Match your hedge to your evidence: strong data supports strong language; preliminary data needs softer claims
Avoid stacking hedges — 'may possibly suggest' hedges the same idea twice

title: A single small pilot study found a promising trend that didn't reach statistical significance. Which claim best matches the evidence?

body.text: “This treatment cures the condition.”
“This treatment may offer modest benefit, though further study is needed.”
“This treatment has no effect whatsoever.”
“This treatment possibly could perhaps help somewhat.”
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

items: Redundant phrases feel formal but add zero information
Every extra word costs the reader attention — spend that attention wisely
Journals enforce strict word limits; redundancy is the easiest place to find space
Cutting redundancy is not about writing less — it's about writing exactly enough

rows: it is important to note that

body.text: PADDED
“Due to the fact that a total of 42 patients were enrolled, it is important to note that the sample size was adequate in order to detect a clinically meaningful difference.”
Same information, roughly 30% fewer words — and easier to read in one pass.
TRIMMED
“Because 42 patients were enrolled, the sample size was adequate to detect a clinically meaningful difference.”

title: “In the present study, we investigated, for the first time, the novel and previously unreported relationship between X and Y.” What can be cut without losing meaning?

body.text: Circle every word you'd delete — 90 seconds

items: “We investigated the relationship between X and Y.”
“Novel,” “previously unreported,” and “for the first time” all claim the same thing — pick one, or let the introduction establish novelty instead
“In the present study” is almost always unnecessary — the reader knows which study this is

title: Which revision best fixes “a total of 15 subjects were recruited for participation in the study”?

body.text: “A total of 15 subjects participated.”
“15 subjects were recruited.”
“Subjects, a total of 15, were recruited for the study.”
No change needed
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

items: Words like 'significant,' 'many,' 'several,' and 'a large proportion' feel scientific but carry no exact meaning
'Significant' especially is dangerous — it has a strict statistical meaning that differs from everyday usage
Whenever you have the actual number, use it instead of a vague quantifier
Reserve 'significant' for statistical significance; use 'substantial' or 'considerable' for a general sense of size

body.text: VAGUE
“A large proportion of participants reported significant improvement in symptoms.”
The revised version separates the proportion (78%) from the statistical claim (p<0.01) — 'significant' is no longer doing double duty.
PRECISE
“78% of participants (39/50) reported symptom improvement, and the difference from baseline was statistically significant (p<0.01).”

items: A paragraph is a group of sentences serving one clear purpose — just like a sentence carries one idea
Start with a topic sentence that states the paragraph's main point
Every following sentence should support, explain, or provide evidence for that point
If a sentence doesn't relate to the topic sentence, it likely belongs in a different paragraph

body.text: Topic Sentence
States the paragraph's single main claim
Supporting Evidence
Data, citations, or reasoning backing the claim
Elaboration
Explains significance or adds necessary nuance
Transition
Links smoothly to the next paragraph's idea

title: You read a paragraph and can't tell what its main point is after the first sentence. What's the most likely cause?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor

items: The topic sentence is missing — the paragraph just starts with a supporting detail
The topic sentence is too general to predict what follows
The paragraph actually contains two ideas and should be split in two

title: Paragraph With No Clear Topic Sentence

body.text: WANDERING
“Participants completed the survey online. Some used mobile devices. The response rate varied by age group. Data were checked for completeness before analysis.”
The revised version opens with the point (completion varied) so every following sentence has a clear job: supporting that claim.
ANCHORED BY A TOPIC SENTENCE

“Survey completion varied by device and age group. Most participants used mobile devices, and response rates were highest among younger age groups. All responses were checked for completeness before analysis.”

title: A paragraph with no topic sentence and several unrelated facts is best fixed by:

body.text: Adding a strong final sentence to summarize
Adding a topic sentence and/or splitting it into focused paragraphs
Converting every sentence to passive voice
Making all sentences the same length
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

items: A transition tells the reader how the next paragraph relates to the one before it
Common relationships: building on a point, contrasting it, or narrowing from general to specific
Avoid mechanical transition words ('Furthermore,' 'Moreover,') as a substitute for real logical connection
The strongest transitions echo a key word or idea from the previous paragraph's last sentence

body.text: MECHANICAL ONLY
“...supports this mechanism. Furthermore, other factors may also be relevant.”
The second version links specific content across paragraphs, not just a generic connector word.
LOGICALLY CONNECTED
“...supports this mechanism. This same pathway may also explain the age-related differences described below.”
One Idea?
Does each sentence make exactly one claim?
No Padding?
Has every redundant phrase been cut?
Right Voice?
Is active/passive chosen deliberately, not by habit?
Clear Topic Sentence?
Does every paragraph open with its main point?
One sentence, one idea — split sentences that try to carry more than one claim
Choose active or passive voice deliberately, based on whether the actor matters
Hunt down and cut redundant phrases — every word should earn its place
Paragraphs need a clear topic sentence and single unifying purpose

title: If a sentence needs to be read twice to be understood, it needs to be rewritten once.

body.text: — A guiding principle for this course
Bring these to our next session

items: Take one paragraph from your own writing (or a draft idea) and split any overloaded sentences
Circle three redundant phrases in something you've previously written and revise them
Bring one sentence you're proud of — we may share a few

title: Building the Introduction and Literature Review

body.text: From broad context to a precise, defensible research question

eyebrow: Branko Aleksic · Dept. of International Medical Education
title: Building the Introduction and Literature Review

body.text: From broad context to a precise, defensible research question
Scientific Writing: Principles and Practice · Honours Student Program

title: By the End of Today, You Can:

items: Structure an introduction as a funnel from broad context to specific aim
Conduct a focused literature review and synthesize — not just list — sources
Identify and articulate a genuine gap in existing knowledge
Write a research question and hypothesis that your study can actually answer

title: The Introduction Is Usually Written Last

items: Most experienced writers draft the introduction after Methods and Results are settled
It's easier to justify a study you've already completed than to predict how to frame one
Don't be discouraged if your first draft of the introduction feels weak — that's normal, not a sign of failure
Today we'll build it piece by piece, so a full draft feels manageable

body.text: 1. Context
Why does this topic matter, broadly?
2. What's Known
Summarize the relevant prior work
3. The Gap
What remains unknown or unresolved?
4. Your Aim
State exactly what you set out to do

items: Start with the clinical or scientific importance of the general topic — not a dictionary definition
Use the opening 2-3 sentences to orient any reader, including one outside your subfield
Avoid starting with 'Since ancient times...' or other overly broad historical openers
Ground the importance in real consequences: disease burden, unresolved clinical questions, cost

body.text: TOO BROAD, NO STAKES
“Diabetes has been studied by scientists for many years and is an important disease that affects many people around the world.”
The stronger version names a real number and a specific consequence — it earns the reader's attention instead of assuming it.
SPECIFIC AND CONSEQUENTIAL
“Type 2 diabetes affects over 400 million adults worldwide and remains a leading cause of preventable cardiovascular disease.”

title: Think of your own research interest. In one sentence, why should a stranger care about it?

body.text: Share your sentence with a neighbor — 90 seconds

items: It names a concrete consequence (health outcome, cost, unresolved risk) — not just 'importance'
It avoids assuming the reader already cares — it earns that interest
It sets up, but doesn't yet answer, the question your study addresses

title: An introduction that opens with 'Since ancient times, disease has affected humanity...' is weak mainly because it:

body.text: Is grammatically incorrect
Is too broad to establish specific, concrete stakes
Uses passive voice
Is too short
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

title: How Much Space for Each Move?

items: As a rough guide for a typical article: context (10-15%), what's known (40-50%), gap (15-20%), aim (10-15%)
A common student mistake is spending too many paragraphs on background and rushing the gap and aim
If your introduction is longer than about one printed page, look for content that belongs in the Discussion instead
The aim should almost always be the introduction's final sentence or two

title: You read an introduction and reach the end still unsure what the study actually tested. What pacing problem does this suggest?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor

title: The Funnel Never Reached Its Point

items: Likely too much space was spent on background, crowding out the gap and aim
Or the aim was stated too vaguely to register as the funnel's narrowest point
Fix: read only your introduction's last two sentences — do they clearly state what you did?
The goal is synthesis, not a list — group studies by theme or finding, not one sentence per paper
Cite the studies most directly relevant to your question, not everything you read
Note where studies agree, where they conflict, and what methods they used
Every citation should do work — advancing the argument toward your gap, not just padding the section

body.text: Listing (Weak)

items: “Smith et al. found X. Jones et al. found Y. Lee et al. found Z.”
Reads like an annotated bibliography
Leaves the reader to draw connections themselves

body.text: Synthesizing (Strong)

items: “Several studies report X (Smith; Jones), though findings on Y remain inconsistent (Lee vs. Chan).”
Groups studies by theme and highlights agreement or conflict
Does the interpretive work for the reader

title: “Reference [12] studied X in mice. Reference [13] studied a related question in rats. Reference [14] used a different method entirely.” What's the underlying problem here?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor

title: It's a List, Not an Argument

items: Each sentence just restates a citation — there's no relationship drawn between them
A synthesized version might say: 'Animal models consistently show X, though findings vary by species and method'
The reader should finish the paragraph understanding the state of the field, not just three isolated facts

title: The primary goal of the literature review section is to:

body.text: List every paper you read during your research
Synthesize prior findings to set up your specific gap
Prove you read more papers than other researchers
Summarize your own results in advance
Vote with a show of hands when prompted
Primary Sources

items: Original research articles reporting new data
The gold standard for supporting specific claims
Always prefer these when citing a specific finding

body.text: Secondary Sources

items: Review articles, textbooks, and summaries of others' work
Useful for background context and orientation
Risky to cite for specific numbers — trace back to the primary source

title: You want to cite a specific statistic (e.g., a prevalence rate). What should you do?

body.text: Cite whichever source mentions the number, even a textbook
Trace the number back to the primary study and cite that
Avoid using specific numbers in the introduction
Cite a review article that references the number
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

items: Start with a focused search in PubMed or a relevant database — use specific terms, not single broad keywords
Prioritize recent, high-quality, peer-reviewed sources; include foundational older work only when necessary
Use reference management software (e.g., Zotero, EndNote, Mendeley) from the very first source you save
Track why each source matters as you save it — you'll forget by the time you write

title: Using a Synthesis Matrix While Reading

items: Before writing, sort your sources into a simple table like the one just shown, organized by theme
This makes conflicts and gaps visually obvious before you write a single sentence
It also prevents the 'list of studies' problem — you're forced to compare, not just record
Update it as you read new sources; it becomes the skeleton of your literature review paragraph

title: The Gap: The Hinge of Your Introduction

items: The gap is the specific thing that remains unknown, untested, or unresolved after your literature review
A strong gap statement often starts with 'However,' 'Despite this,' or 'It remains unclear whether...'
The gap must follow logically from what you just summarized — it can't come out of nowhere
A vague gap ('more research is needed') is not a gap — it's an admission you haven't found one yet

title: Four Common Kinds of Research Gaps

body.text: Population Gap
Studied in one group (e.g., adults) but not another (e.g., adolescents)
Conflicting Evidence
Existing studies disagree, and the reason for disagreement is unclear
Methodological Gap
Prior studies used weak designs; a stronger method hasn't been applied
Contextual Gap
Findings from one setting (e.g., country, era) may not generalize
NOT ACTUALLY A GAP
“Further research is needed to better understand this topic.”
The strong version names exactly who hasn't been studied and why that matters — a reader immediately understands what your study will add.
A GAP YOU CAN ACT ON
“No prior study has examined this intervention in adolescents, despite its established efficacy in adults.”

title: Draft one sentence naming a gap in a topic you're interested in. Start with 'However,' or 'It remains unclear whether...'

body.text: Write it down — we'll ask a few volunteers to share

items: Does it follow logically from evidence you just cited, or does it appear out of nowhere?
Is it specific enough that your own study could plausibly close it?
Would a reader in your field immediately understand why it matters?

title: The Aim: The Narrowest Point of the Funnel

items: State your specific aim, research question, or hypothesis in direct, unambiguous language
Common openers: 'This study aimed to...', 'We hypothesized that...', 'We tested whether...'
The aim should map directly onto the gap you just identified — no surprises
This is often the very last sentence of your introduction

body.text: Introduce a new topic not covered earlier in the introduction
Map directly onto the gap identified just before it
Be broad enough to allow multiple different studies
Be saved for the Discussion section instead
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

items: P — Population
Who is being studied? Be specific about age, condition, setting
I — Intervention (or Exposure)
What is being tested, given, or observed?
C — Comparison
Compared to what — placebo, standard care, another group?
O — Outcome
What specific outcome are you measuring, and when?

body.text: PICO is especially useful for clinical and epidemiological research questions — it forces precision on all four elements at once.

rows: Adults aged 18–40 with newly diagnosed stage 1 hypertension
Usual care with no structured exercise program
Change in systolic blood pressure at 8 weeks

title: Using PICO, sketch a clinical research question in your area of interest. Can you fill in all four elements?

body.text: Write it down — 2 minutes, then a few volunteers share

title: If a Box Was Hard to Fill In...

items: A missing Comparison often means the question isn't yet testable as designed
A vague Population or Outcome usually means the aim needs to be narrowed further
PICO is a diagnostic tool as much as a planning one — gaps in the table reveal gaps in the question

rows: “How does sleep duration relate to exam performance?”
You can predict a specific direction
“We hypothesized that shorter sleep duration is associated with lower exam scores.”
“This study aimed to characterize the relationship between sleep and academic outcomes.”

body.text: NOT TESTABLE
“This study aimed to explore issues related to sleep and academic performance.”
A testable aim names the variables, the population, and what relationship you're checking — anyone could design a study to answer it.
TESTABLE AND SPECIFIC
“This study aimed to determine whether average nightly sleep duration predicts final exam scores among second-year students.”

title: Trade your gap sentence from earlier with a neighbor. Can they write a matching aim statement from it?

body.text: Swap papers — 2 minutes

title: If They Struggled to Write an Aim...

items: Your gap may be too vague or too broad to act on directly
Try narrowing it: which population, which variable, which comparison exactly?
A good test: could someone design a study from your gap statement alone?

body.text: IMPRECISE
“We hypothesized that sleep affects academic performance.”
A precise hypothesis names the groups being compared and the expected direction of the effect — it can be clearly supported or refuted by data.
PRECISE AND TESTABLE
“We hypothesized that students averaging fewer than 6 hours of sleep would score significantly lower on final exams than those averaging 7–8 hours.”
The introduction funnels from broad context to a precise aim in four deliberate moves
A literature review synthesizes and groups sources — it doesn't just list them
A real gap is specific, follows from the evidence, and is closeable by your study
Your aim or hypothesis should map directly onto the gap you identified

title: An introduction should make the reader feel the gap before you ever state your aim.

body.text: — A guiding principle for this course
Bring these to our next session

items: Draft a 4-move introduction outline for your own research interest (context, known, gap, aim)
Find one published introduction and label its four moves
Bring one figure or table from a paper you found genuinely easy to understand

body.text: Next: Class 4 — Presenting Results and Discussion
Reporting findings objectively, then interpreting them honestly

eyebrow: Branko Aleksic · Dept. of International Medical Education
title: Presenting Results and Discussion

body.text: Reporting findings objectively, then interpreting them honestly
Scientific Writing: Principles and Practice · Honours Student Program

title: By the End of Today, You Can:

items: Report results objectively, in a logical order, without interpretation
Design figures and tables — and write captions — that stand on their own
Build a discussion that interprets, contextualizes, and honestly limits your findings
Cite sources correctly and avoid the most common forms of plagiarism
State what was observed — numbers, directions, statistical significance
Save every 'this suggests,' 'this proves,' or 'this means' for the Discussion
Order findings logically: usually primary outcome first, then secondary outcomes
Every claim needs a number attached — exact values, confidence intervals, p-values

body.text: INTERPRETS TOO EARLY
“The treatment group had fewer complications, demonstrating that the new protocol is safer and should replace the current standard of care.”
“Demonstrating” and “should replace” are judgments — the Results section reports the numbers and lets the Discussion make the case.
STAYS OBJECTIVE
“Complications occurred in 4 of 50 patients (8%) in the treatment group, compared with 12 of 50 (24%) in the control group.”

title: “Mean recovery time was 3.2 days shorter in the intervention group (95% CI: 1.1–5.3, p=0.004).” Is this Results-appropriate, or does it cross into interpretation?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor

items: It reports a measured difference with a confidence interval and p-value — pure observation
No claim is made about why, or what it means for practice
Compare: 'This shorter recovery suggests the intervention accelerates healing' would belong in Discussion

title: Which phrase is most likely to signal that a sentence has drifted from Results into Discussion?

body.text: “Mean age was 42.3 years (SD 8.1)”
“This suggests that older patients respond better”
“15 of 60 participants withdrew before follow-up”
“Figure 2 shows the distribution of scores”
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

title: What a Complete Result Statement Includes

rows: Lets readers judge the actual magnitude
Shows precision, not just a point estimate
Lets readers verify the analysis was appropriate

items: A result showing no significant difference is still a result — report it with the same rigor as a positive one
Never omit outcomes just because they didn't reach significance — this distorts the scientific record
State the actual finding: 'No significant difference was observed (p=0.34)' rather than implying nothing happened
Selective reporting of only favorable results is a serious research integrity issue
Most clinical studies open their Results with a table comparing baseline characteristics between groups
This lets readers judge whether randomization or group selection produced comparable groups
Typically includes age, sex, and other variables relevant to the outcome being studied
Differences in Table 1 don't need p-values in most modern guidelines — describe them narratively instead
Lead with the primary outcome — the result your study was designed to answer
Follow with secondary outcomes, in the order they were introduced in the Methods
Group related findings together rather than jumping between topics
Use subheadings for long Results sections to help readers navigate

title: When to Use a Figure vs. a Table

items: Use a figure
To show trends, patterns, distributions, or comparisons visually
Use a table
To present precise numbers a reader may want to look up or compare directly
Never present the exact same data in both a figure and a table — pick the format that serves the point
Every figure and table should be understandable before the reader returns to your main text

title: Writing a Caption That Stands Alone

items: A caption should let a reader understand the figure without reading the surrounding paragraph
Structure: what is shown → key methodological detail → how to read any symbols or error bars
Define every abbreviation used in the figure, even if defined elsewhere in the text
State the sample size and any statistical test directly in the caption when relevant

body.text: CAN'T STAND ALONE
“Figure 1. Results of the study.”
The strong caption tells a reader exactly what's plotted, the sample size, and how to interpret the symbols — no need to hunt through the text.
SELF-CONTAINED
“Figure 1. Mean systolic blood pressure (mmHg) at baseline and 12 weeks by treatment group (n=50 per group). Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals; *p<0.05 vs. control.”

title: You have a bar chart comparing 3 groups' average scores, with error bars and one significant comparison marked with an asterisk. Draft a caption for it.

body.text: Write one or two sentences — 2 minutes

items: What is plotted, and the units of measurement
Sample size for each group
What the error bars represent (SD, SE, or 95% CI — they are not interchangeable)
What the asterisk or symbol means, and the significance threshold used

title: The same dataset should generally be presented:

body.text: In both a figure and a table, for redundancy
In whichever single format best serves the reader's need
Only in a table, never a figure
Only as raw numbers in the text
Vote with a show of hands when prompted
Legible Labels
Axis labels and units large enough to read at presentation size
No Clutter
Remove gridlines, 3D effects, or extra elements that don't add information
Purposeful Color
Color encodes meaning, not decoration — and works in grayscale too
Consistent Scale
Axis ranges chosen to represent the data honestly, not exaggerate effects

title: A Misleading Axis vs. an Honest One

body.text: TRUNCATED AXIS
A bar chart starting the y-axis at 90% instead of 0% makes a 2-point difference look like a dramatic gap.
Truncated axes are one of the most common ways figures unintentionally — or intentionally — mislead readers.
FULL, HONEST AXIS
The same chart with a y-axis starting at 0% shows the true, modest size of the difference between groups.

title: You see a bar chart with a y-axis that starts at 80 instead of 0, making a small difference look dramatic. What should you, as a careful reader, do?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor

title: Read the Axis Before the Bars

items: Always check axis start and end values before judging the size of an effect visually
Recalculate the real percentage difference from the numbers, not the bar heights
As an author, this is exactly the habit to build into your own figure design from the start

title: Four Moves of a Strong Discussion

body.text: 1. Restate
The main finding, in plain language
2. Compare
To prior literature — agreement or conflict
3. Limit
Honest, specific study limitations
4. Signify
Why this finding matters going forward

items: State clearly whether your finding agrees or disagrees with previous studies
When results conflict with prior work, propose a plausible reason — don't just note the conflict
Avoid cherry-picking only the studies that support your conclusion
This is where your literature review from Class 3 pays off — you already know the landscape

title: What Counts as a Real Limitation

body.text: Sample
Small size, single site, or a population that limits generalizability
Design
Observational design, no control group, or short follow-up
Measurement
Imperfect tools, self-report bias, or missing data
Confounding
Variables you couldn't fully control or measure
TOO VAGUE TO BE USEFUL
“This study has some limitations that should be considered.”
A vague limitation statement signals the author hasn't seriously considered the study's weaknesses — reviewers notice this immediately.
SPECIFIC AND HONEST
“This single-center study enrolled only 45 participants, which may limit generalizability to broader populations.”

title: Why might a researcher be tempted to hide or minimize a study's limitations? What's the risk of doing that?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor — 90 seconds

items: Reviewers and readers will find weaknesses whether or not you name them — naming them first shows rigor
Hidden limitations that surface later can undermine trust in your entire paper
A well-stated limitation often strengthens a paper — it shows you understand your own evidence

title: Which of these is the strongest limitation statement?

body.text: “There may be some limitations to this work.”
“Our study, like all studies, is not perfect.”
“Because participants self-reported diet, recall bias may have affected accuracy.”
“Limitations are discussed elsewhere.”
Vote with a show of hands when prompted
Clinical Relevance
How might this change practice, if it holds up?
Scientific Relevance
What does it add to the theoretical picture?
Future Directions
What specific next study would extend this work?

title: A strong closing to a Discussion section should generally:

body.text: Introduce new results not mentioned earlier
Repeat the abstract word for word
State the finding's significance and plausible next steps
End abruptly after the limitations
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

items: Citations let readers verify your claims and trace the evidence you built on
Under-citing implies an idea is yours when it isn't — even unintentionally, this is a serious issue
Over-citing common knowledge clutters the text and dilutes citations that truly matter
Follow your target journal's citation style consistently from your very first draft

body.text: Direct Copying
Using another author's exact words without quotation marks and citation
Patchwriting
Swapping a few words in someone else's sentence while keeping its structure
Self-Plagiarism
Reusing your own previously published text without disclosure
PATCHWRITING
“Original: 'Exercise reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease in older adults.' Patchwrite: 'Physical activity lowers the risk of heart disease in elderly people.'”
Patchwriting keeps the original sentence structure with synonyms swapped in — that's still considered plagiarism. Real paraphrase reconstructs the idea in your own sentence, with a citation.
GENUINE PARAPHRASE + CITATION
“Regular physical activity is a well-established protective factor against cardiovascular disease in aging populations (Author, Year).”

title: You want to use a striking sentence from a paper almost word-for-word. What are your two honest options?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor

items: Quote it directly, in quotation marks, with a citation — used sparingly in scientific writing
Paraphrase it fully in your own sentence structure and vocabulary, with a citation
What's not an option: changing a few words while keeping the original structure and calling it your own

title: Reusing a paragraph you wrote in a previous paper, without citation, in a new manuscript is:

body.text: Always acceptable since you wrote it
A form of self-plagiarism that should be avoided or properly disclosed
Only a problem if someone else notices
Required practice for consistency
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

items: Save the full citation the moment you read a source — don't rely on finding it again later
Use reference management software consistently so in-text citations and the reference list stay synchronized
Double-check every automatically generated citation — software occasionally introduces errors
Keep a short note on why each source matters; it saves enormous time when drafting

body.text: Results report objectively; save interpretation entirely for the Discussion
Figures and tables — and their captions — should stand alone without the main text
A strong Discussion restates, compares, honestly limits, and signifies your findings
Cite carefully: genuine paraphrase and clear attribution protect your credibility

title: A limitation stated plainly is a strength; a limitation hidden is a liability waiting to be found.

body.text: — A guiding principle for this course
Bring these to our next session

items: Draft a Results paragraph (real or hypothetical data) with zero interpretive language
Write one figure caption that could stand completely on its own
List two honest limitations for a study you're planning or reading about

body.text: Next: Class 5 — Editing, Peer Review, and Beyond
Revising your own work, responding to reviewers, and reaching wider audiences

eyebrow: Branko Aleksic · Dept. of International Medical Education
title: Editing, Peer Review, and Beyond

body.text: Revising your own work, responding to reviewers, and reaching wider audiences
Scientific Writing: Principles and Practice · Honours Student Program

title: By the End of Today, You Can:

items: Self-edit a draft systematically, at the structure, paragraph, and sentence level
Give and receive peer feedback that actually improves a manuscript
Understand the peer review process and respond to reviewer comments professionally
Translate technical findings into a plain-language summary for non-expert audiences
Proofreading catches typos and grammar errors — the very last step
Editing questions structure, logic, and clarity — it happens much earlier, and repeatedly
Never edit and draft at the same time — finish a rough draft first, then revise in passes
Expect to revise a paper many times; even experienced researchers do

body.text: 1. Structure
Are sections and paragraphs in a logical order?
2. Paragraph
Does each have one clear topic sentence?
3. Sentence
Is every sentence clear, active, and free of redundancy?

items: Read it aloud
Awkward phrasing is much easier to hear than to see
Set it aside for a day
Distance makes your own errors visible again
Read only the topic sentences of every paragraph in order
This should reveal the paper's argument on its own
Reverse outline your draft
Write down what each paragraph actually does — compare it to what you intended

title: Take a paragraph you wrote recently (for this course or elsewhere). Read only its first sentence. Does it predict what follows?

body.text: Check silently — we'll discuss patterns as a group

items: If the first sentence doesn't predict the paragraph, the topic sentence may be missing or buried
If you can't summarize the paragraph's point in one phrase, it may be carrying too many ideas
This 'topic sentence test' is one of the fastest structural edits you can run

title: Which editing pass should generally happen first?

body.text: Sentence-level grammar and word choice
Structure and overall logical order
Formatting the reference list
Checking figure resolution
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

rows: Does each section do its IMRAD job, in order?
Does each paragraph have one clear topic sentence?
Is every sentence active, precise, and non-redundant?

title: Editing Tools: Helpful, Not a Replacement

items: Grammar and style checkers catch typos and basic errors — useful, but not a substitute for structural editing
AI writing tools can help you brainstorm phrasing, but you remain responsible for accuracy and originality
Never let a tool rewrite technical claims without verifying they still say exactly what you mean
The three-pass checklist above is something no automated tool can fully do for you
Start with what's working — it orients the writer and isn't just politeness
Be specific: 'this paragraph has two ideas' beats 'this is unclear'
Distinguish major issues (structure, logic, missing evidence) from minor ones (wording, typos)
Ask questions rather than issuing commands — it respects the writer's ownership of the text

body.text: VAGUE AND UNACTIONABLE
“This section is confusing. Please fix it.”
Actionable feedback names the specific problem and points toward a specific fix, without rewriting the sentence for the author.
SPECIFIC AND ACTIONABLE
“This paragraph moves between the sample and the outcome measure without a clear transition — consider splitting it into two paragraphs.”

title: How does it feel to receive feedback that's just “this is unclear” versus feedback that names exactly what's unclear?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor — 90 seconds

items: Vague feedback creates anxiety without giving a path forward
Specific feedback feels collaborative, even when it points out a real problem
As you review classmates' drafts later this term, aim for feedback you'd want to receive yourself
Read all feedback once fully before reacting to any single comment
Assume good intent — a reviewer's job is to strengthen your paper, not attack you
You don't have to agree with every comment, but you should understand why it was made
If a comment is confusing, ask a clarifying question rather than guessing

title: The most useful peer feedback tends to be:

body.text: General praise, to keep morale up
Specific, tied to a location in the text, and actionable
A full rewrite of the author's sentences
Focused only on grammar and spelling
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

items: Open with one or two genuine strengths — this isn't padding, it tells the writer what to keep
Group remaining comments by priority: structural issues first, then paragraph-level, then sentence-level
Limit yourself to the 3-5 most important issues rather than marking every possible improvement
Close by naming the single change that would most improve the draft if the writer only had time for one

title: Imagine a classmate's introduction has a strong opening but never clearly states a gap or aim. How would you phrase that feedback?

body.text: Draft one or two sentences of feedback — 2 minutes

items: “Your opening effectively establishes why this topic matters. The introduction would be stronger with an explicit gap statement — right now it moves from background straight to your methods.”
Notice: names what works, names the specific structural issue, and points to where it's missing
This is feedback the writer can act on immediately

body.text: Submit
Manuscript enters the editorial system
Editor Screen
Checked for fit and basic quality
Peer Review
2–3 experts evaluate rigor and importance
Decision
Accept, revise, or reject
Revision
You respond to reviewer comments
Accept
Rare on a first submission — the paper needs no further changes
Major Revision
Substantial changes needed; resubmission will be re-reviewed
Minor Revision
Small, clearly specified changes requested
Reject
Not a fit for this journal, or fundamental issues found

items: Address every single comment, even ones you disagree with — silence reads as avoidance
Structure your response point by point, quoting the original comment before your reply
When you disagree, explain your reasoning respectfully and with evidence — you can push back
Clearly state what changed in the manuscript, and where (e.g., 'Added to Discussion, paragraph 2')

body.text: DEFENSIVE
“The reviewer clearly did not read our manuscript carefully. This point is already obvious.”
Even a frustrating comment deserves a measured, constructive reply — editors read these exchanges closely.
PROFESSIONAL
“We thank the reviewer for this comment. We have clarified this point in the Methods (page 4, paragraph 2) to avoid ambiguity.”

title: A reviewer asks you to run an additional analysis you believe is unnecessary. How would you respond, in principle?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor — 90 seconds

items: Explain clearly why you believe the analysis isn't necessary, with reasoning or evidence
Offer an alternative if one exists (e.g., a sensitivity analysis instead)
If the reviewer's concern is valid but the specific request isn't, address the underlying concern

title: When you disagree with a reviewer's comment, the best approach is to:

body.text: Ignore the comment in your response
State your disagreement with clear reasoning and remain respectful
Argue that the reviewer is unqualified
Withdraw the manuscript
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

rows: Shows exactly what you're responding to
States exactly where and what was revised
Thankful, concise, and professional — even under criticism

items: A preprint is a manuscript shared publicly before (or alongside) formal peer review
Speeds up sharing of findings, invites early feedback, and establishes priority of discovery
Clearly labeled as not yet peer-reviewed — readers should treat conclusions cautiously
Check your target journal's policy on preprints before posting, though most major journals now allow it

body.text: No Real Review
Accepts almost anything quickly, with little genuine peer review
Fee-Driven
Aggressively solicits submissions and charges high, mandatory fees
Poor Indexing
Not indexed in reputable databases like PubMed or Scopus

title: You receive an email inviting you to submit to a journal you've never heard of, promising publication within 5 days. What would you check before submitting?

body.text: Discuss with a neighbor — 90 seconds

items: Is the journal indexed in PubMed, Scopus, or Web of Science?
Does it have a genuine editorial board with identifiable, reachable experts?
Is peer review timeline realistic — genuine review almost never takes days?
When in doubt, ask your supervisor or check a journal evaluation tool before submitting
Patients, funders, journalists, and policymakers rarely read the full paper — they read a summary
Many journals and funding bodies now require a plain-language summary alongside the abstract
This is not 'dumbing down' — it's translating precisely, without jargon, for a different expert: the reader
Practicing this skill also sharpens how well you understand your own findings

body.text: Technical Abstract

items: “An 8-week aerobic exercise intervention significantly reduced systolic blood pressure (−8.2 mmHg, 95% CI: −11.4 to −5.0, p<0.001) in adults with stage 1 hypertension.”
Assumes statistical literacy and field-specific vocabulary

body.text: Plain-Language Summary

items: “Adults with mildly high blood pressure who walked briskly for 30 minutes, most days, for 8 weeks saw a meaningful drop in their blood pressure.”
Keeps the key finding, drops the statistics and jargon

title: Take the sentence: “The intervention group demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in HbA1c (−0.6%, p=0.02) relative to controls.” Write a one-sentence plain-language version.

body.text: Draft it on paper — 2 minutes

items: “People who received the treatment had noticeably better blood sugar control than those who didn't.”
Notice what's gone: the exact percentage, the p-value, the technical outcome name
What stayed: the direction of the effect and who it applied to — the parts a general reader actually needs

body.text: Include every statistic from the abstract
Preserve the key finding while removing jargon and statistics
Be written before the technical abstract
Replace the need for a full abstract
Vote with a show of hands when prompted

items: A growing number of researchers share findings via short posts or threads on academic social platforms
The same principle applies as with plain-language summaries: precise translation, not oversimplification
Never claim more certainty in a post than your actual evidence supports — this is where overreach spreads fastest
Link back to the original paper so interested readers can verify the full context

body.text: Full Paper
Complete technical detail for expert peers
Abstract
Condensed technical summary for quick scanning
Plain-Language Summary
Key finding, no jargon, for the public
Social Post
One clear sentence, linked back to the source

title: Scientific Writing Is a Lifelong Skill

items: Every skill from this course — structure, clarity, honest interpretation, careful revision — applies far beyond a single paper
You'll use it in grant applications, clinical documentation, and every future manuscript
The habits (one idea per sentence, funnel introductions, objective results) get faster with practice, not easier to skip
Your assignments for this course are a chance to practice all of it on work that matters to you

body.text: Edit in passes — structure, then paragraphs, then sentences — never all at once
Give feedback that's specific and actionable; receive it with curiosity, not defensiveness
Respond to peer reviewers point by point, professionally, even when you disagree
Plain-language summaries translate your findings precisely for a different audience
Classes Complete
From IMRAD structure to peer review — you now have a full toolkit for scientific writing

title: The best scientific writers are not the ones who get it right the first time — they are the ones who revise the most honestly.

body.text: — A guiding principle for this course
Carrying these skills forward

items: Complete your final short writing assignment, applying all five classes
Exchange drafts with a classmate for structured peer review
Revisit your Class 1 sample article — try re-labeling it with everything you now know

body.text: Thank you for an engaged and thoughtful five sessions
